ls.start.menu.title: The Omarchy menu
ls.start.menu.body:
SUPER + SPACE is the one key to remember. The menu is the front door to almost everything: apps, themes, backgrounds, capture, system actions, setup wizards.
If you forget how to do something, open it and read down the list rather than hunting for a command.
You can extend it yourself in ~/.config/omarchy/extensions/omarchy-menu.jsonc, which hot-reloads on save.
ls.start.apps.title: Opening things
ls.start.apps.body:
SUPER + ALT + SPACE is the app launcher: type a few letters, press Enter.
The common ones have their own keys. SUPER + RETURN gives you a terminal, SUPER + SHIFT + RETURN a browser, SUPER + SHIFT + N your editor.
From a script or a terminal, omarchy launch browser does the same thing, so your own keybindings can reuse Omarchy's launchers.
ls.start.keys.title: Every keybinding, on screen
ls.start.keys.body:
SUPER + K opens the full keybinding cheat sheet, read straight from your live Hyprland config — so it shows your edits, not the defaults.
SUPER + ESCAPE is the system menu: lock, suspend, restart, shut down.
This plugin's tutorial covers the keys worth memorising; the cheat sheet covers all of them.
ls.start.bar.title: The bar and its panels
ls.start.bar.body:
The strip across the top is the Omarchy shell. Every icon on it opens a panel, and every panel has a keybinding too, so you never have to aim at a 20-pixel icon.
SUPER + CTRL + A for audio, + N for network, + B for bluetooth, + P for power, + D for displays.
Inside a panel, j and k move, Enter activates, Tab moves to the next panel along the bar, Escape closes.
ls.start.cli.title: The omarchy command
ls.start.cli.body:
Everything the menu does, the omarchy CLI does too, and it is self-documenting.
omarchy commands lists all of them. omarchy <group> --help narrows it to one group, like omarchy theme --help.
That is the fastest way to find out whether something you want already exists — it usually does.
ls.start.notifications.title: Notifications
ls.start.notifications.body:
Notifications stack in the top corner and fade on their own.
SUPER + comma dismisses the last one — or invokes it, if it has an action worth taking.
SUPER + SHIFT + comma clears the lot. SUPER + SHIFT + ALT + comma opens the history, for the one you dismissed too fast.
ls.windows.focus.title: Moving focus
ls.windows.focus.body:
Windows tile automatically; you move between them with SUPER and an arrow key, in the direction you want to go.
ALT + TAB walks the windows on the workspace in order, ALT + SHIFT + TAB walks back.
Nothing here moves a window — it only changes which one is listening to your keyboard.
ls.windows.move.title: Rearranging windows
ls.windows.move.body:
Add SHIFT to the focus keys and the window comes with you: SUPER + SHIFT + arrow swaps it with its neighbour.
SUPER + J flips how the next window will split, so you decide whether it lands beside or below.
SUPER + W closes the focused window (SUPER + Q does the same, if you have the muscle memory).
ls.windows.size.title: Resizing, floating, fullscreen
ls.windows.size.body:
SUPER + minus and SUPER + equals resize the focused window. Add ALT for finer steps, CTRL for coarse ones.
SUPER + F is fullscreen. SUPER + ALT + F stretches it the full width without going fullscreen.
SUPER + T lifts a window out of the tiling into a floating one, and drops it back.
ls.windows.workspaces.title: Workspaces
ls.windows.workspaces.body:
SUPER + 1 through 9 jump straight to a workspace. SUPER + SHIFT + a number sends the focused window there.
SUPER + TAB and SUPER + SHIFT + TAB step through them in order; SUPER + CTRL + TAB flips back to the one you were just on, which is the one you actually want most of the time.
The workspace indicators on the bar fill in as you use them.
ls.windows.layouts.title: Workspace layouts
ls.windows.layouts.body:
Each workspace has its own layout, and SUPER + L cycles it (SUPER + ALT + L goes back).
Tiled layouts arrange everything for you. The floating layout leaves windows where you put them and brings up the dock.
It is per-workspace on purpose: keep your editor tiled and your design workspace floating.
ls.windows.scratchpad.title: Scratchpad, Quake console, dock
ls.windows.scratchpad.body:
SUPER + S shows and hides the scratchpad — a workspace that floats over whatever you are doing. SUPER + ALT + S throws the focused window into it.
SUPER + backtick drops down a Quake-style console from the top of the screen.
SUPER + M minimises a window to the dock, which you will find on floating workspaces.
ls.windows.groups.title: Grouping windows into tabs
ls.windows.groups.body:
SUPER + G groups the focused window with its neighbour, turning two tiles into one tabbed stack.
SUPER + ALT + TAB cycles the tabs inside the group. SUPER + ALT + an arrow pulls a window into the group on that side.
SUPER + ALT + G takes the active window back out again.
ls.windows.monitors.title: More than one screen
ls.windows.monitors.body:
SUPER + SHIFT + CTRL + an arrow moves the focused window to the monitor in that direction; SUPER + SHIFT + ALT + an arrow moves the whole workspace.
CTRL + ALT + TAB moves focus to the next monitor without touching any windows.
Which monitor is where, and at what resolution, is set in ~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua.
ls.look.themes.title: Themes
ls.look.themes.body:
A theme in Omarchy is the whole desktop at once: the bar, terminals, the editor, the background, GTK apps.
SUPER + CTRL + T opens the picker. From a terminal, omarchy theme set catppuccin or omarchy theme next.
To tweak a stock theme without losing it on the next update, drop an edited colors.toml in ~/.config/omarchy/themes/<theme-name>/ and re-apply the theme.
ls.look.background.title: Backgrounds
ls.look.background.body:
SUPER + CTRL + SPACE opens the background switcher for the current theme, with previews.
Each theme ships its own set, so switching themes switches the pool of backgrounds too.
Drop your own images into the theme's backgrounds directory and they show up in the picker.
ls.look.font.title: Fonts
ls.look.font.body:
One monospace font drives the bar, the terminals and the menus. omarchy font list shows what is installed, omarchy font set "<name>" switches it.
Pick a Nerd Font if you want the icons on the bar to keep rendering — they are glyphs in the font, not images.
The setting lands in ~/.config/fontconfig/fonts.conf and the shell picks it up on its own.
ls.look.textsize.title: Making everything bigger
ls.look.textsize.body:
omarchy display text size 1.25 scales text across the shell, GTK apps and terminals in one go — the right knob for a high-DPI screen or tired eyes.
omarchy display text size reset puts it back.
For one monitor only, set its scale in ~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua instead.
ls.look.gaps.title: Gaps, borders, transparency
ls.look.gaps.body:
SUPER + SHIFT + BACKSPACE toggles the gaps between windows off and on — the fastest way to reclaim screen space.
SUPER + BACKSPACE makes the focused window transparent, which is handy for reading something behind it.
For permanent changes to gaps, border width and rounding, edit ~/.config/hypr/looknfeel.lua; Hyprland reloads on save.
ls.look.bar.title: Rearranging the bar
ls.look.bar.body:
The bar has five sections along it: left, centerBegin, center, centerEnd, right — plus the tray drawer.
omarchy bar move omarchy.clock --section right moves a widget; omarchy bar position bottom moves the whole bar.
Anything the commands do not cover, you can edit directly in ~/.config/omarchy/shell.json under bar.layout. It hot-reloads on save. Keep widgets out of center unless you want the clock pushed off-centre.
ls.look.nightlight.title: Night light
ls.look.nightlight.body:
omarchy toggle nightlight warms the display now, and remembers the state across reboots.
For a schedule rather than a toggle, edit the profiles in ~/.config/hypr/hyprsunset.conf and run omarchy restart hyprsunset.
SUPER + CTRL + ALT + W is unrelated but nearby: it toggles the weather readout on the bar.
ls.capture.screenshot.title: Screenshots
ls.capture.screenshot.body:
PRINT takes a smart screenshot — it guesses between region, window and screen from what you do next.
omarchy capture screenshot region or … windows or … fullscreen picks explicitly, and takes copy or save after that.
By default the image goes to the clipboard and to ~/Pictures.
ls.capture.record.title: Screen recordings
ls.capture.record.body:
ALT + PRINT starts a recording of a region; add --fullscreen on the command line for the whole screen.
It keeps going until you stop it: omarchy capture screenrecording --stop-recording, or the indicator on the bar.
Flags cover desktop audio, the microphone, and a webcam overlay — see omarchy capture --help.
ls.capture.ocr.title: Text out of anything on screen
ls.capture.ocr.body:
SUPER + CTRL + PRINT draws a region and runs OCR over it, putting the text on your clipboard.
It is the answer to an error message in a screenshot, a serial number in a photo, or a code in a video call.
Same thing from a terminal: omarchy capture text.
ls.capture.color.title: The colour picker
ls.capture.color.body:
SUPER + PRINT turns the cursor into an eyedropper and copies the hex value of whatever you click.
It reads any pixel on screen, not just inside a particular app.
Useful when you are building a theme and want a colour you can already see.
ls.capture.share.title: Sharing and converting
ls.capture.share.body:
SUPER + CTRL + S shares a file — it uploads and hands you back a link.
SUPER + CTRL + PERIOD transcodes a video or image into something smaller or more portable.
Both are the same tools the capture flows use, so a recording can go straight out without a round trip through a file manager.
ls.capture.clipboard.title: Clipboard and emoji
ls.capture.clipboard.body:
Omarchy keeps a clipboard history: SUPER + CTRL + V opens it, filter by typing, Enter pastes.
It holds images as well as text, so a screenshot you took three screenshots ago is still there.
SUPER + CTRL + E opens the emoji picker, which works the same way.
ls.config.where.title: Where your settings live
ls.config.where.body:
Two directories are yours: ~/.config/hypr/ for the window manager, and ~/.config/omarchy/ for the shell, themes and extensions.
One directory is not: /usr/share/omarchy/ belongs to the package, and anything you change there is overwritten by the next omarchy update. Read it freely — it is the best documentation there is — but make your changes under ~/.config/.
Everything in ~/.config/hypr/ and ~/.config/omarchy/ reloads when you save it. No restarts, no daemon juggling.
ls.config.bindings.title: Adding your own keybinding
ls.config.bindings.body:
Bindings live in ~/.config/hypr/bindings.lua and are written in Lua: o.bind("SUPER + E", "Files", { omarchy = "nautilus" }) adds one; o.rebind(…) replaces an existing one instead of fighting with it.
Check what is already taken with SUPER + K before you pick a key.
After saving, hyprctl reload applies it and hyprctl configerrors tells you if you got the syntax wrong.
ls.config.monitors.title: Monitors and resolutions
ls.config.monitors.body:
~/.config/hypr/monitors.lua is where you set each display's resolution, refresh rate, position and scale.
hyprctl monitors prints what Hyprland currently sees, including the exact names to use — start there rather than guessing.
Scale is per-monitor, which is how you mix a HiDPI laptop panel with a regular external screen.
ls.config.shell.title: shell.json: the bar, panels, idle
ls.config.shell.body:
~/.config/omarchy/shell.json configures the Omarchy shell. bar holds the layout and each widget's own settings; idle holds the screensaver and lock timers.
It only needs the keys you want to change — everything else falls through to the defaults in /usr/share/omarchy/config/omarchy/shell.json, which is worth reading once.
Saving the file hot-reloads the shell. If something ever fails to apply, omarchy restart shell.
ls.config.idle.title: Idle, screensaver, lock
ls.config.idle.body:
In shell.json, idle.screensaver and idle.lock are seconds of idle time. "Lock after ten minutes" is "lock": 600.
Set either to 0 to turn it off entirely.
SUPER + CTRL + L locks right now, without waiting for the timer.
ls.config.plugins.title: Shell plugins
ls.config.plugins.body:
Every bar widget and panel is a plugin — including this one. omarchy plugin list shows what is installed and what is enabled.
To change how a built-in widget behaves, do not edit the packaged copy: omarchy plugin clone omarchy.workspaces copies it to ~/.config/omarchy/plugins/ under your own name and points the bar at your copy, which survives updates.
Anything you save under ~/.config/omarchy/plugins/ reloads automatically.
ls.config.hooks.title: Running your own scripts on events
ls.config.hooks.body:
Hooks let your script run when Omarchy does something: omarchy hook install theme-set ~/bin/retint-my-app runs it every time the theme changes.
They land in ~/.config/omarchy/hooks/, one directory per event, so several scripts can share an event.
omarchy hook list shows what is installed and which events are available.
ls.care.update.title: Updating
ls.care.update.body:
omarchy update updates Omarchy and the system together, and runs any migrations that come with the new version.
Run it in a terminal rather than from a button: it may ask you things, and you want to see what it says.
If an update changes a config file you have edited, the migration leaves your version in place and tells you.
ls.care.packages.title: Installing software
ls.care.packages.body:
omarchy pkg add <name> installs from the Arch repos; omarchy pkg aur add <name> from the AUR.
omarchy install covers the curated bundles — omarchy install docker sets up more than just the package.
The menu has the same thing under Install, with a list to pick from if you do not know the package name.
ls.care.debug.title: When something is wrong
ls.care.debug.body:
omarchy debug --no-sudo --print gathers version, hardware, theme, monitor and service state into one block you can read or paste into a bug report. Always pass both flags; without them it waits on a password prompt.
For a crash, omarchy agent crash walks the core dump with a coding agent.
Start here before changing anything — it is faster than guessing.
ls.care.reset.title: Getting back to defaults
ls.care.reset.body:
omarchy refresh shell backs up your current shell.json and drops the default back in; omarchy refresh hyprland does the same for the window manager. omarchy refresh config hypr/bindings.lua resets one file.
Each one takes a timestamped backup first, so a reset is recoverable — but it is still a reset, which is why there is no button for it here.
If you only want to undo your last edit, look in the backup beside the file before reaching for this.
ls.care.reminders.title: Reminders
ls.care.reminders.body:
omarchy reminder 15 "Pickup Jack" puts a desktop notification 15 minutes out. SUPER + CTRL + R asks for one interactively.
omarchy reminder show lists what is pending, omarchy reminder clear drops them all.
They survive a shell restart, so a long reminder is safe.
ls.care.restart.title: Restarting pieces
ls.care.restart.body:
Most config reloads on save, so you rarely need this — but when the bar gets stuck, omarchy restart shell brings it back without touching your session.
omarchy restart terminal reloads open terminals after a config change, and there is a restart for most other services too.
If a plugin edit does not appear, omarchy-shell shell rescanPlugins forces the reload.
